concepts.name: Geological Origin and Age of the Peninsular Plateau
key_dimensions: Formation from Gondwanaland and its tectonic significance
Composed of ancient crystalline, igneous and metamorphic rocks — among the oldest landmasses on Earth
Distinction between Archaean gneisses/schists vs. Deccan Traps (much younger volcanic overlay)
UPSC trap: Why is it considered a 'stable' block despite being part of an active tectonic plate?

concepts.name: General Structure and Physiographic Character of the Peninsular Plateau
key_dimensions: Broadly triangular shape tilted slightly westward vs. dominant eastward drainage — resolving the paradox
Average elevation range (~600–900 m) and its variation across sub-divisions
Residual/relict nature of the plateau and peneplanation concept
UPSC trap: Distinguishing a 'plateau' from a 'plain' using the Peninsular Plateau as a case study

concepts.name: Central Highlands (Malwa Plateau, Bundelkhand, Baghelkhand)
key_dimensions: Extent: north of Vindhyas to the Aravalli fringe — boundary demarcation
Malwa Plateau's structural tilt and its role in Chambal, Betwa, Ken river flow patterns
Difference between Malwa Plateau, Bundelkhand Upland, and Baghelkhand — often confused in prelims
UPSC trap: Whether Central Highlands are part of the Deccan Plateau or a separate physiographic unit

concepts.name: Deccan Plateau — Extent, Boundaries and Sub-divisions
key_dimensions: Bounded by Satpura-Vindhya in the north, Western Ghats in the west, Eastern Ghats in the east
Internal sub-divisions: Maharashtra Plateau, Karnataka Plateau (Mysore), Telangana Plateau
Difference in rock type, elevation, and drainage between sub-divisions
UPSC trap: 'Deccan Plateau' used loosely vs. its precise physiographic boundary — Narmada as northern boundary controversy

concepts.name: Deccan Trap — Formation, Extent and Significance
key_dimensions: Volcanic origin: fissure eruptions during Late Cretaceous–Early Eocene (~65 Ma, K-Pg boundary)
Extent of lava flows (~5 lakh sq. km) covering parts of Maharashtra, MP, Gujarat, Karnataka
Black cotton soil (Regur) derived from Deccan Traps — agricultural and economic significance
UPSC trap: Deccan Traps ≠ entire Deccan Plateau; significant portions of Deccan Plateau are NOT covered by Traps

concepts.name: Vindhya and Satpura Ranges — Structure, Orientation and Significance
key_dimensions: Vindhyas: a scarp/fault-block range vs. Satpuras: a horst block — tectonic distinction
Satpura Range as a watershed between Narmada (rift valley, flows west) and Son-Tapti drainage
Role as a historical and cultural divide between North and South India
UPSC trap: Satpura and Vindhya are often conflated — their relative positions (Satpura SOUTH of Narmada; Vindhya NORTH of Narmada)

concepts.name: Narmada and Tapti Rift Valleys — Tectonic Origin and Drainage Anomaly
key_dimensions: Graben/rift valley formation due to faulting — contrast with typical river valleys formed by erosion
West-flowing drainage of Narmada and Tapti as an anomaly in the eastward-tilted plateau
Why Narmada and Tapti do not form deltas despite being major rivers — structural reason
UPSC trap: Narmada flows through a rift valley but is NOT a consequent stream; it is a structurally controlled river

concepts.name: Western Ghats (Sahyadri) — Structure, Continuity and Passes
key_dimensions: Escarpment (fault scarp) on the western side vs. gentle eastern slope — asymmetric cross-section
Continuity and breaks: Palakkad (Palghat) Gap, Thal Ghat, Bhor Ghat — strategic and climatic significance
Western Ghats as a watershed: rivers flowing east (Godavari, Krishna, Cauvery) vs. west (short, rapid)
UPSC trap: Western Ghats are NOT fold mountains; they are the uplifted/faulted edge of the Deccan Plateau

concepts.name: Eastern Ghats — Discontinuous Nature, Structure and Comparison with Western Ghats
key_dimensions: Discontinuous, dissected ranges vs. continuous Western Ghats — reason: cut by eastward-flowing rivers
Lower elevation (~600 m avg.) compared to Western Ghats (~1500 m avg.)
Meeting point of Eastern and Western Ghats at Nilgiri Hills — the 'confluence' concept
UPSC trap: Eastern Ghats do not act as a significant orographic barrier unlike Western Ghats — climatic implication

concepts.name: Nilgiri, Anaimalai, Cardamom Hills — Southern Extensions and Highest Peaks
key_dimensions: Nilgiris as the junction of Western and Eastern Ghats — unique biodiversity hotspot
Doddabetta (Nilgiris) vs. Anaimudi (Anaimalai/Western Ghats) — highest peaks of South India and Peninsula
Cardamom Hills (Idukki) as the southernmost extension of Western Ghats
UPSC trap: Anaimudi (~2695 m) is the highest peak of the Peninsular Plateau AND of South India — not Doddabetta

concepts.name: Aravalli Range — Age, Orientation and Relevance to Plateau Boundary
key_dimensions: Among the oldest fold mountains in the world (Pre-Cambrian) — now eroded into residual hills
NE-SW orientation acting as a boundary between the Peninsular Block and the Great Plains
Rain shadow effect: Aravallis' failure to block Arabian Sea moisture — Thar Desert formation
UPSC trap: Aravallis run PARALLEL to the Arabian Sea monsoon winds, not perpendicular — hence poor orographic rainfall

concepts.name: Chota Nagpur Plateau — Structure, Mineral Wealth and Drainage
key_dimensions: Composed of ancient Gondwana rocks and Archaean basement — Damodar Valley coal fields
Described as the 'Ruhr of India' — concentration of iron, coal, mica, copper
Part of the northeastern extension of the Peninsular Plateau — often excluded from 'Deccan Plateau'
UPSC trap: Damodar River flows EASTWARD (not westward) despite being in a rift/graben-like valley — drainage anomaly

concepts.name: Meghalaya/Shillong Plateau — Detached Fragment of the Peninsular Block
key_dimensions: Geologically a northeastward extension of the Peninsular Block, separated by the Garo-Rajmahal Gap
Shillong Plateau: composed of ancient gneisses and granites similar to Peninsula
Cherrapunji/Mawsynram orographic rainfall — role of plateau in creating one of the world's wettest spots
UPSC trap: Meghalaya Plateau is NOT part of the Himalayas or Northeast Hills (Purvanchal) — it is a Peninsular outlier

concepts.name: Drainage Pattern of the Peninsular Plateau — Antecedent, Superimposed and Consequent Rivers
key_dimensions: Eastward tilt explaining Godavari, Krishna, Mahanadi, Cauvery flowing east into Bay of Bengal
Dendritic drainage pattern on homogeneous Deccan lava surfaces vs. trellis/rectangular on structural terrain
Peninsular rivers as non-perennial (rain-fed, no glacial source) — significance for water security
UPSC trap: Narmada and Tapti are the major exceptions to eastward drainage — structural (rift) not gradient control

concepts.name: Coastal Plains Adjoining the Peninsular Plateau — East vs. West Coast
key_dimensions: Western Coastal Plain: narrow (10–25 km), steep gradient, no major deltas, emergent coast — Konkan, Malabar
Eastern Coastal Plain: wider (100–130 km), gentle gradient, major deltas (Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna, Cauvery) — submergent coast
Difference in coast type: Western = rocky, cliff-lined; Eastern = sandy, lagoons (Chilika, Pulicat, Kolleru)
UPSC trap: Konkan coast lies between Daman & Goa; Malabar coast lies between Goa & Kanyakumari — precise boundary matters

concepts.name: Soil Types of the Peninsular Plateau and Their Lithological Linkage
key_dimensions: Black cotton soil (Regur) — derived from Deccan Traps, high moisture retention, suited for cotton
Red and yellow soils — derived from crystalline/metamorphic rocks of Peninsular gneisses (Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Odisha)
Laterite soils — formed under high rainfall + leaching on plateau surfaces (Kerala, Karnataka plateau edges)
UPSC trap: Laterite soils are POOR in fertility despite forming in high-rainfall areas — leaching removes nutrients

concepts.name: Gondwana Coal Fields of the Peninsular Plateau
key_dimensions: Damodar Valley, Mahanadi Valley, Godavari Valley, Son Valley — distribution pattern along ancient rift basins
Gondwana coal (~250 million years old) vs. Tertiary coal of NE India — age and quality difference
Why Gondwana coalfields are located in valleys/basins within the plateau — tectonic subsidence and preservation
UPSC trap: Most of India's coal (~98%) is Gondwana coal, NOT Tertiary; Tertiary coal is found in NE India (Assam, Meghalaya)

concepts.name: Physiographic Boundary: Peninsular Plateau vs. Indo-Gangetic Plain
key_dimensions: The 'Great Boundary Fault' (Aravalli) and the Rajmahal Hills as northern/northeastern limits
Transition zone: presence of older alluvium (Bhangar) and buried peninsular rocks beneath the plains
Delhi Ridge as a northward extension of Aravallis into the Indo-Gangetic Plain — a UPSC favourite
UPSC trap: The boundary is NOT a sharp line — peninsular rocks are buried under alluvium and reappear as isolated outcrops (e.g., Rajmahal Hills)

concepts.name: Palakkad (Palghat) Gap — Formation, Significance and UPSC Traps
key_dimensions: Only major break in the Western Ghats — ~32 km wide, ~300 m elevation (significantly lower than surrounding Ghats)
Formed due to differential erosion along a fault zone — structural origin
Climatic significance: allows moisture-laden SW monsoon winds to penetrate into Tamil Nadu's rain-shadow zone
UPSC trap: Palghat Gap is in Kerala (between Nilgiris and Anaimalai Hills), NOT in Karnataka — precise location tested

concepts.name: Tectonic Stability vs. Seismic Activity in the Peninsular Plateau
key_dimensions: Generally considered a stable, rigid block (craton) — but intraplate earthquakes occur (Latur 1993, Koyna 1967)
Koyna earthquake linked to Reservoir-Induced Seismicity (RIS) — dam-related trigger
Latur earthquake in Deccan Trap region — exposed myth of complete peninsular seismic stability
UPSC trap: Peninsular India falls in Seismic Zones II and III — NOT entirely 'earthquake-free'; distinction from Himalayan Zones IV and V
